subtitle: An annotated list of RFCs numbered 600 through 699.

tldr.problem: Readers needed a compact status report on RFCs in the 600–699 number range.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists each number with available author, date, title, and a short annotation; entries also identify RFC numbers that were not issued.
tldr.outcome: It serves as an index and brief guide to the listed RFCs, rather than defining a protocol.

today: RFC 699 is an Informational index of RFCs 600 through 699. It does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: How to Read the Summary
sections.content:
RFC 699 describes itself as a slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs numbered 600 through 699. Each row gives the RFC number, author, date, and title; some rows add a short note about the document.

The list also marks numbers that were not issued.
sections.plainLanguage: This document is an index to one hundred RFC numbers. It gives brief identifying details and short notes for many entries.

sections.title: Topics in the Number Range
sections.content: The annotations cover a range of subjects, including Telnet options, FTP revisions, IMP/Host protocol changes, host-name services, network measurements, and administrative schedules. Some entries refer readers to related RFCs or say that a later document is the current version of an earlier note.
sections.plainLanguage: The listed documents cover protocol changes, network operation, and administrative topics. The notes point out some links between documents in the range.

sections.title: Purpose and Status
sections.content: RFC 699 calls the list a kind of status report on RFCs 600 through 699. It is an Informational document and does not define a protocol or prescribe network behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a reference list, not a protocol specification. It summarizes documents in the stated number range.
